title: Global Variables, static and Linkage
summary: Globals exist for the whole run of the program. **Linkage** decides whether other `.cpp` files can see a name. A `static` local keeps its value between calls. Avoid globals that can change.
markdown:
## Global variables A variable defined outside every function is **global**. Any function below it in the file can use it. ```cpp #include int g_score{ 0 }; void addPoints() { g_score += 10; } int main() { addPoints(); std::cout << g_score << '\n'; // 10 return 0; } ``` | | Local variable | Global variable | |---|---|---| | Scope | Its block | The rest of the file | | Lifetime | Until its block ends | The whole run: created before `main`, destroyed after it | | If you give no value | Unpredictable | Zero | Here scope and lifetime separate. This lifetime is called **static storage duration**. The `g_` prefix is a common convention that marks a name as global. > [!danger] Avoid globals that can change > When any function anywhere can modify `g_score`, a wrong value makes **every** function a suspect. A function that only uses its parameters can be understood and tested on its own. Pass values in as arguments and hand results back with `return`. > > Global **constants** are fine. Nothing can change them, so nothing can break them. ## Linkage: can other files see it? Scope is about one file. In a program with several `.cpp` files there is a further question: can a name defined in one file be used from another? That property is **linkage**. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph A["a.cpp"] a1["int shared{ 5 };
external linkage"] a2["static int secret{ 7 };
internal linkage"] end subgraph B["b.cpp"] b1["extern int shared;
can use it"] b2["secret
cannot be reached"] end a1 -.-> b1 ``` | Linkage | Meaning | |---|---| | **External** | One shared thing that every file can refer to | | **Internal** | Private to this file. Another file may use the same name for something else. | What you write at file level decides which you get: | Written outside any function | Linkage | Typical use | |---|---|---| | `void helper();` or a function definition | external | Functions other files call | | `int counter{ 0 };` | external | (A changeable global: avoid) | | `static void helper()` | internal | A helper that only this file needs | | `namespace { void helper() {} }` | internal | The modern way to say the same | | `constexpr int limit{ 5 };` | internal | A constant used in one file | | `inline constexpr int limit{ 5 };` in a header | external | **A constant shared by many files** | To use another file's external variable you declare it with `extern`: "this exists, and it is defined somewhere else". The usual place for such declarations is a header. ## `inline`: defined in a header, without breaking the rule You met the One Definition Rule in [[1.08 Multiple Files and Headers]]: a definition may appear only once in the program. A header is pasted into every file that includes it, so anything **defined** in a header would break that rule. `inline` is the exception. It tells the linker: "this definition will turn up in several files; they are all the same one." ```cpp // constants.h #pragma once namespace constants { inline constexpr double gravity{ 9.81 }; inline constexpr int maxPlayers{ 4 }; } ``` This is the standard way to share constants. It is also why the `Random` helper in [[3.04 Random Numbers]] used `inline`. ## `static` locals: a function with a memory Put `static` on a **local** variable and it gets the long lifetime of a global while keeping the small scope of a local. ```cpp #include int nextId() { static int s_id{ 0 }; // initialized once, the first time through return ++s_id; } int main() { std::cout << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << '\n'; // 1 2 3 return 0; } ``` | Call | `s_id` before | `s_id` after | |---|---|---| | first | 0 | 1 | | second | 1 | 2 | | third | 2 | 3 | An ordinary local would be created afresh at 0 on every call. Only `nextId` can touch `s_id`, which makes this far safer than a global counter. ## One word, several meanings `static` is the most overloaded keyword in C++. Its meaning depends on where it appears. | Where | Meaning | |---|---| | On a local variable | Lives for the whole run and keeps its value between calls | | On a global variable or function | Internal linkage: private to this file | | On a class member | Shared by all objects of the class: [[6.05 Static Members and Friends]] | ## Check yourself ```quiz ? How does a `static` local differ from an ordinary local? - It can be used from any function + It is initialized once and keeps its value between calls - It cannot be changed after it is created - It is created again on every call, like a parameter > A `static` local lives for the whole program, so it remembers its value between calls. Its scope is still just the function. ? How should a constant be shared across several files? - As a plain global variable in one `.cpp` file - As a `static` variable inside `main` + As an `inline constexpr` variable in a header, inside a namespace - Copied by hand into every file that needs it > `inline constexpr` in a header gives every file the same constant without breaking the one-definition rule. ? What is the difference between internal and external linkage? - Internal linkage is for functions; external linkage is for variables - Internal names are faster to call than external ones + An external name is one thing shared by every file; an internal name is private to its own file - There is none; both are visible to every file > External linkage means every file refers to the same entity. Internal linkage (for example `static` at file level) keeps a name private to one file. ? Why are changeable global variables a problem? - They use more memory than local variables - They cannot be initialized - The compiler copies them into every function + Any function can change them, so bugs are hard to trace > Anything anywhere can change a non-const global, which makes bugs hard to track down. Constants are fine. ```
ideas:
1. Write `int callCounter()` with a `static` local that counts how many times it has been called.
2. Create `constants.h` with `inline constexpr` values and use them from two `.cpp` files.
3. Make a `static` helper function in one `.cpp` file and try to call it from another. Read the linker error.

cards.q: How does a `static` local differ from an ordinary local?
cards.a:
It is initialized once and keeps its value between calls

A `static` local lives for the whole program, so it remembers its value between calls. Its scope is still just the function.

cards.q: How should a constant be shared across several files?
cards.a:
As an `inline constexpr` variable in a header, inside a namespace

`inline constexpr` in a header gives every file the same constant without breaking the one-definition rule.

cards.q: What is the difference between internal and external linkage?
cards.a:
An external name is one thing shared by every file; an internal name is private to its own file

External linkage means every file refers to the same entity. Internal linkage (for example `static` at file level) keeps a name private to one file.

cards.q: Why are changeable global variables a problem?
cards.a:
Any function can change them, so bugs are hard to trace

Anything anywhere can change a non-const global, which makes bugs hard to track down. Constants are fine.
